Fort McMurray braces for another boom

This oil town has known tremendous prosperity, but also hardship and tragedy. A decade after layoffs and wildfire, Fort Mac is gearing up for a new wave of growth

By
Graison Foster
November 2, 2026 at 6:00 a.m.
Last Updated: November 5, 2026 at 3:11 p.m.
Listen to audio version of this article
Sponsored by
0:00 / 19:25
Instaread

Jobs in Fort McMurray start early. At 6 a.m. the sky is still dark, and the dining area of the hotel is already full. A television blares the morning news, and the men sit apart at separate tables, heads down, in bulky winter coats with safety vests pulled over them, shovelling in their breakfast.

At the coffee dispenser, a man fills a stainless steel to-go mug. Beyond the tall glass doors, the parking lot is jammed with pickup trucks, shoulder to shoulder, their sides and tires streaked with dirt. Last night, it took several rounds in the lot to find a space.

The men at these tables are here for the work, and the pay is how Fort McMurray came to be called Fort McMoney.

Estella Petersen is one of the people who came for it, and she is plain about why. “There’s no way I could make what I’m making anywhere in Canada other than up here,” she said. Taxes take “like 37 per cent” of her pay, she figures. “We pay a lot to live here, but we earn a lot, too.”

Petersen stands 5-foot-1. Long beaded earrings hang down into her mid-length brown hair. Like much of the town, she is dressed fully in denim, down to a heavy jacket. She offers a handshake and a warm smile as she speaks softly.

Petersen drives a dozer for the oilsands, a remote region of northern Alberta that has bestowed enormous wealth on her province, her town and her family. When she stands beside her machine, it towers over her.

Over coffee in the hotel, she said she has run heavy equipment in Fort McMurray for almost 17 years through the last boom, the bust that followed and the fire that burned everything she owned.

And now, she said, “everyone seems to be revving up.”

All over this oil town, the talk is of opportunity. The young woman who brings supper to the table at a local restaurant has moved here from Kelowna, B.C., to train in power engineering and take a shot at a six-figure salary. A woman pouring coffee at Tim Hortons has come all the way from Greece, and when asked why, she answers in one word: money.

The college has wait lists; houses are drawing multiple offers again, and more big box stores are on their way.

Forces far removed from this northern enclave are working in its favour. War in the Middle East choked off oil moving through the Strait of Hormuz. And suddenly Ottawa and Alberta, normally at odds with one another, are shaking hands on a new oil pipeline to the West Coast.

This oilsands outpost has known tremendous prosperity, the hard years of belt-tightening that followed and the 2016 wildfire that emptied this place. With all of that behind it, there is a realization that the next wave of wealth may not rise as high as the last one.

Petersen has heard the same talk. “Everyone thinks this pipeline is going to go through. Everyone’s hiring people, like everything’s ramping up.

“And they think we’re going to have a bit of a boom here.”

Second growth

On a Sunday in mid-October, traffic is light on Highway 63, the main road into Fort McMurray. The freshly paved blacktop lies pristine under a bright blue sky. Pines stand among the aspen. The last leaves have turned yellow and many trees are bare. Along the road, the trees the fire killed remain charred, and small spruce have come up among them. Suddenly, the highway drops down a long, steep hill, and the town lies in the valley below, past a bridge over the low Athabasca River.

To a first-time visitor, the scars that the fire left behind are still evident. Petersen laughs at the idea. “I was thinking it looks pretty good now,” she said.

Petersen lived through it. The fire chief at the time, Darby Allen, called the inferno the Beast. On May 3, 2016, families scrambled to grab what they could, loaded pets and pieces of their lives into their vehicles and escaped. As the convoy of residents fled down Highway 63, the only road out, walls of flames climbed the trees on both sides of the road, and the thick smoke and ash turned the sky black.

Entire neighbourhoods looked as if a tornado had gone through, except it was the fire that flattened everything in its path. Vehicles sat burned and smoldering where they had been abandoned. More than 88,000 people were forced out and for thousands, home was gone.

Petersen remembers being told not to worry. Just as quickly, the order came to evacuate. “And then all of a sudden it’s like, get out.”

She lost her home. “You hear those stories of people with one backpack,” she said. “I had one backpack.”

Her motorcycle was gone, too, along with “absolutely everything.” She had no insurance on her contents. Today she owns two condos in Fort McMurray, and her son lives in one.

For all the fire took from her, the town suits her. “I just feel like it’s a great environment up here,” she said. “I really enjoy it up here. It does feel like home to me.”

In the hotel lobby, Petersen thinks back to the life she left to come north. Before Fort McMurray, she was working two and a half jobs. “I thought, why am I killing myself doing this when my friends are working in Fort Mac, coming home and buying big-ticket items and stuff?”

When she talked to her friends about moving here, some were skeptical. “Half of them said, no, you can’t come up there. You’re a female … You’re native; like, you won’t make it up there. And I was like, challenge accepted.”

Petersen’s roots are in Cowessess First Nation in southern Saskatchewan. She grew up between Manitoba and Alberta, part of that time in a small town where she said she faced racism and a challenging childhood.

Over the years, she had worked as an armed guard for Brink’s, a probation officer and a corrections officer. “I’ve always sought out jobs that are atypical of females.”

So, she went to look for work up north in the oilsands. “I contacted at least, I don’t know, 20 places,” she said. “And only one of them responded to me.” That company trained her on haul trucks, then laid her off three weeks later along with dozens of others. She landed another job within a few days, and she has stayed in the industry ever since.

She proved her friends wrong. For Petersen, Fort McMurray is a place where an Indigenous woman can get ahead. “I think the oilsands really accepts and encourages Indigenous business. I think here you see more affluent Indigenous people than you would, you know, in other parts of Canada. And for me, I feel welcome here.”

She pushes back when people say that all Indigenous people oppose pipelines. “Well, no, we’re not, because … some of us have a lot of connection with the oilsands.”

Some people have called her colonized for the life she chose. “I just want a better life for myself and my kids … It doesn’t mean you have to leave your culture behind,” she said. “I think you can have both your culture and a well-paying job in the oilsands.”

Petersen spent the last decade rebuilding her life. Now she is looking ahead. Her son has followed her into the oilsands, running heavy equipment for a contractor and hopes to be hired by one of the big companies. She has noticed more hiring around town and likes his chances.

“I’m sure it’ll happen soon.”

The town shares her outlook. It is busy now but is counting on bigger years ahead.

A college called ‘We’

At the entrance to Keyano College, the poles of a tipi frame stand on a lawn strewn with fallen leaves, under trees nearly stripped of theirs. In nêhiyawêwin, the Cree language, the name is kiyânaw, which means “we, us, our.” The college began in 1965 in three ATCO trailers, as the Alberta Vocational Centre. Today it trains heavy equipment operators and welders and offers nursing and education degrees with partner universities.

Mark Dolmont, Keyano’s vice-president, academic, first came to Fort McMurray in the early 2000s, when there were more fly-in workers than there are now. “You used to go to restaurants and have to wait forever, and people were throwing money,” he said. “You didn’t have that sense of community.” Over the past 20 years, he feels the town has grown closer.

He is frank about why people move here. “Do I think a lot of people initially have come for money? Absolutely, and I think it’s just opportunity.”

Keyano once leaned heavily on international students and now puts more of its focus on locals with the aim of keeping graduates in town. “If they’re from the community, they’re educated in the community, there’s a high chance they’re gonna stay in the community.”

Renie Dela Paz is the kind of student Keyano hopes to keep. He arrived in Fort McMurray from the Philippines with his family in 2018, two years after the wildfire. He worked first, then enrolled in Keyano, where he graduated last year in hospitality management. Now in the first year of a second program, the governance and civil studies diploma, he is president of the student association.

The hospitality program gave him a chance to work in the accommodation department at an oilsands site, and the talk there is upbeat. He hears “a lot of positive things” about a boom coming. There are “some hurdles,” he said, but he sees good things ahead.

Many Keyano programs have wait lists. Beyond the trades, the college has put more focus on healthcare, and demand for nursing is well beyond the seats available, according to Dolmont. The heavy equipment technician program has about 188 people waiting, and the steam fitter and welder program has 89. He cannot say for sure who hires the most graduates, though Suncor Energy Inc. and then Syncrude Canada Ltd. are the obvious guesses, and much of the work ends up in the oilsands whichever company they join.

In the pipeline

In a hotel ballroom, leaders of six Métis nations in Wood Buffalo stood in a row against a gold-papered wall. They had called a news conference at the last minute, and they had a complaint to make. The mood in the room was frustration and disappointment but not opposition.

“Anything done without us is actually against us,” Ruby Ladouceur, president of Fort Chipewyan Métis Nation, told reporters and members of Métis communities who came to hear the leaders speak on the proposed West Coast pipeline.

Much of the hope in Fort McMurray rests on the Pacific Link oil pipeline that would carry up to one million barrels of oil a day from Bruderheim, Alta., to a proposed terminal in Delta, B.C., and filling it would take growth in the oilsands.

The Métis leaders gathered here are not against the pipeline itself. They worry about what that growth could mean for their six communities that span from Fort Chipewyan in the north to Conklin in the south, and for the land and water they depend on.

The leaders said they were left out of the pipeline talks, and they want in. Ottawa promised Indigenous communities at least a 10 per cent stake in the pipeline. Kelly Myers, district captain of Fort McMurray Métis District 17, said she did the math for the Métis. “Zero per cent of 10 per cent is zero per cent.”

Far beyond Fort McMurray, world events are pushing the pipeline forward. U.S. President Donald Trump’s tariffs showed Canada it leans too much on one buyer. About 90 percent of Canada’s crude exports went to the United States last year, according to the Canada Energy Regulator. Prime Minister Mark Carney won the last election promising to make Canada an energy superpower, and support for new pipelines grew. Then war in the Middle East sent Asian refiners looking for oil they could count on. In Canada, only the oilsands can produce enough to feed that demand.

Production is already climbing. S&P Global Energy, a U.S. firm, expects the oilsands to average a record 3.5 million barrels a day this year, three percent more than last year.

Some producers have started spending on growth again after a decade of restraint, most of them smaller companies in conventional and thermal heavy oil. Fort McMurray wants the big oilsands companies to follow.

Petersen doubts Pacific Link can move quickly. Alberta’s Cold Lake First Nations filed in Federal Court on Oct. 8 a challenge to Ottawa’s decision to designate the pipeline a project in the national interest. “I think if it went through, it would be, like, maybe six or seven years from now. Because now they’re in court. So then that has to roll through the system. How are they gonna push that through quickly?

When all of this will land is the million-barrel question. Shaz Merwat, Royal Bank of Canada’s energy policy lead, said, “Everyone’s kind of still pointing to a pipeline becoming operational in 2032, 2033.” A start with shovels in the ground in 2027 would be “ambitious,” though the process has already gone “a lot faster” than he expected.

Thick skin

Petersen gets up at 5:25 a.m. for work. The shift is 12 hours, and the drive is an hour each way, so the day runs to 14. She works three days and three nights, then has six days off. “I love that shift, actually.” Many people work seven days and seven nights, then seven days off. By the seventh night, she said, “you’re already into that system. It’d be hard to get out of it.”

Women were rare on the crews when she started. “I could probably count them on both my hands.” Now, by her own guess, they make up “probably 40, maybe even 50 per cent” of her company.

Asked how the men treated her in the early years, Petersen said, “You have to have thick skin for sure.” Fort McMurray is a blue-collar town, in her words, with “kind of some redneck ideologies,” though “I think times are changing here for sure.”

She sees it in who gets hired. “I see not just natives being hired. I see, like other nationalities being hired. So, that’s good, too.”

The machines are also changing. Petersen runs her dozer in the autonomous area of the mine, where she has worked for eight or nine years. There, giant haul trucks move with no one in the cab, steering themselves by GPS while operators in a control room watch over the fleet. She was one of about 14 people there at the start, and now she said it takes about half the crew.

Whatever growth comes next could need fewer people than last time around. A mine or a well now runs on a smaller crew, and some of the machinery moves with no one sitting in the driver’s seat.

Taking the town’s pulse

Fort McMurray’s wealth is quiet. Median family income in the Regional Municipality of Wood Buffalo, which includes Fort McMurray, was $185,400 in 2023, the second highest in Alberta, according to the provincial government.

Lisa Hartigan, a realtor for Coldwell Banker United, has sold homes in Fort McMurray for 25 years. “You can always feel when Fort McMurray is going to make a turn, and it’s usually very quick,” she said. “I do think that we’re going to have another boom.”

Any market has highs and lows, but now Hartigan is busier than ever. Data from the Alberta Real Estate Association show August sales in Fort McMurray were up about eight per cent from a year earlier, with the number of homes for sale down by a quarter.

Hartigan does not think this one will be as robust as the last, though she is hopeful. This year she sees “multiple offers, lower inventory and people getting out and buying now.”

Fort McMurray’s real estate market has had a hard run. The oil price crash in late 2014 triggered a painful recession in Alberta. The wildfire struck in 2016 and downtown flooded in 2020. Hartigan feels the mood is lifting. “This year we can really feel it again that there’s some positivity because it’s just been so negative for so long,” she said.

Petersen remembers the rents of her first years north. She paid $1,250 for a room with a bathroom in the hallway. Could rent climb that high again? “I don’t think it’ll get that high again, but you never know,” she said.

Growth has strained Fort McMurray before. A University of Alberta study published in 2015 tied the town’s long housing shortage and expensive rents to the rapid expansion of oilsands mining. It found the homelessness rate doubled the next-highest in Alberta.

Some people in Fort McMurray have no home at all. The municipality’s last count in October 2025 was at 205, up from 152 the year before. Toni Elliott, acting director of community services for Wood Buffalo, sees no single cause. “Factors can include the availability of housing. Sometimes the rental screening requirements, such as credit check,” she said.

The municipality now has a landlord liaison who works with new tenants and their landlords. “It’s been a very successful program,” Elliott said.

If the population climbs and the money starts to flow, Fort McMurray will be watching its crime numbers. Wood Buffalo saw about 17 per cent fewer crimes last year than 2024, according to RCMP figures published by the municipality. Property crime fell by about 22 per cent.

Years away

What Fort Mcmurray pulls out of the ground leaves town and keeps going. Oil and natural gas end up in more than 6,000 everyday products and high-tech devices, from lipstick to laptops, and the trucks that carry them run on diesel.

Like oil, some of the town’s young people want to venture into the world. Jade Gillgower, who is in her early 20s, has worked for almost two years at The Treasure Chest, a women’s boutique in the Peter Pond Mall. Her parents came to Fort McMurray from Zimbabwe in 2001, and she is the first of the family born in Canada. Her father is a millwright, and the move was “more for the work.”

Gillgower wants to see a community on the rise but is not sure her future is here. “Inflation and everything is just getting crazy. Gas is crazy.” She plans to study criminology at the University of Alberta, starting in the fall of 2027, and does not know whether she will come back. “I feel like there’s probably more opportunities in the bigger cities.”

Petersen, however, isn’t going anywhere, yet. She thought about leaving earlier, but “it would be stupid to leave a well-paying job,” she said. She gets out of town for somewhere warm when she can. “I like Mexico.” A couple of years ago she drove to Mazatlán and stayed a month. “It’s my favourite place.” When she retires, she wants to be a snowbird.

Until then, “I would like to see one more boom.”

Graison Foster
Graison Foster covers energy and business from Edmonton. Raised on a farm in central Alberta, she previously worked at Global News in Vancouver and at CBS2 in Palm Springs. She also spent three years in Dubai, where she owned a luxury real estate brokerage.
